subject: Business Models
title: Brand Licensing
description: A short lesson to help you apply Brand Licensing.

hook.text: Disney earns $5 billion/year from licensing alone. Characters on lunchboxes, pajamas, and backpacks.

buildup.text: Licensees pay 5-15% royalty on wholesale for the right to put Mickey Mouse on their products.

discovery.text: Disney creates the character once, then earns royalties forever from thousands of manufacturers.

twist.text: Luxury brands like Ferrari license their name for theme parks and clothing—sometimes damaging exclusivity.

climax.text: Brand licensing is pure margin: no manufacturing, no inventory, just a name on a contract.

punchline.text: Build the brand once, license it forever. Names print money.

quiz.question: What risk does excessive licensing pose to luxury brands?

details.summary: Brand licensing allows companies to earn revenue by permitting third parties to use their brand name, characters, or intellectual property on products they manufacture and sell. Disney earns billions licensing characters to toy makers, clothing brands, and theme park merchandise.
details.whyItMatters: Brand licensing generates high-margin revenue from existing intellectual property without manufacturing risk. It extends brand reach into product categories the company would never enter directly while licensees handle production and distribution.
takeaways: Companies earn royalties by licensing their brand to third-party manufacturers
Licensing generates revenue without production costs or inventory risk
Brand owners must carefully control quality to protect brand value

faq.question: How are brand licensing deals typically structured?
faq.answer: Licensees pay an advance against future royalties, then ongoing royalties of 5% to 15% of wholesale revenue. Contracts specify product categories, territories, quality standards, and minimum sales guarantees. Licensors retain approval rights over designs and marketing materials.

faq.question: What risks does brand licensing create for the brand owner?
faq.answer: Poor-quality licensed products damage brand perception. Overexposure through too many licensed products can dilute brand exclusivity. Licensees may underinvest in quality to maximize margins. Monitoring and enforcing quality standards across many licensees requires significant resources.
